name: Language of Lord North's Island, called by the natives Tobi, as pronounced by Horace Holden and Benjamin Nute
catalog_citation: Pickering, John. 1845. Memoir on the Language and Inhabitants of Lord North's Island [in the Indian Archipelago; with a Vocabulary]. Memoirs of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, new series 2: 205-247. Cambridge: Metcalf & Co.
catalog_locator: p. 236, orthographic note at the head of 'A Vocabulary of the Language of Lord North's Island, called by the Natives Tobi' (note begins p. 235).
catalog_quote: The consonants have their ordinary English sounds; but the g is always hard, as in game, get, give, &c. The accentual marks only denote the syllable on which the stress of the voice is to be laid, and not a modification of the vowel sound. The accentual stress is always on the penultimate, except where otherwise denoted by the accentual mark.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Tobi material as pronounced by Holden and Nute and written down by Pickering, word stress falls on the penultimate syllable by default; words that deviate are individually marked with an accent in the vocabulary (about 18 of c. 113 headwords, most of them final-stressed, e.g. tukkalek' 'back', tumma' 'bad', petchem' 'foot', nibo' 'night', arreng' 'yellow'; a few initial, e.g. mish'ium 'belly', ka'imuk 'hand').
new_statements.exceptions: Exceptions are not described as a class but marked word by word with an accent; in the 1845 vocabulary roughly 18 headwords carry a non-penultimate mark, predominantly on the final syllable, a few on the initial syllable of trisyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms (isolated vocabulary items and short dialogue sentences) as remembered and pronounced by two American seamen after two years on Tobi (1832-34); the statement is framed as a transcription convention (unmarked = penultimate) rather than an analysed phonological rule, and Pickering himself warns (1836 appendix, p. 122) that the forms are 'approximations' not furnished by natives.
new_statements.identity_note: Pickering (1836, 1845) and Hale (1846) present the material as 'the language of Lord North's Island / Tobi', i.e. they intend Tobian (tobi1238), but every form was supplied from memory by the American captives Horace Holden and Benjamin Nute; this Holden corpus (vocabulary + five dialogues) is exactly what Glottolog's hora1238 'Horace Holden's Pidgin Tobi' denotes (Grant 2014 argues it is a reduced/pidginised Tobian with Malay, Palauan and possibly Spanish admixture; Hale 1846 already notes the sentences 'can hardly be relied upon as showing the real idiom'). The stress statement therefore describes the pidgin as pronounced by Holden/Nute, not modern Tobian (for which see Quackenbush 1968, Capell 1969 on Sonsorol-Tobi under tobi1238).

sources.note: p. 236, orthography note heading the Vocabulary: accentual marks denote the stressed syllable only; 'The accentual stress is always on the penultimate, except where otherwise denoted by the accentual mark.' About 18 headwords carry an exception mark (mostly final: tukkalek', tumma', vitching', makkrazm', shibbo', petchem', nibo', buzhanet', arreng'; a few initial: mish'ium, ka'imuk, mi'tchimum); the rest (c. 95, many monosyllabic) are unmarked = penultimate.
